title: Use language and communication in occupational learning programmes

lessons.title: Learning strategies for adult learners
lessons.html:
Becoming an active learner

An occupational learning programme, such as a learnership in plant production, seed production or meat examination, mixes classroom or online learning with practical work on the farm or in the plant. Success depends not only on what is taught, but on how you learn. This unit helps you use language and communication to learn well.

Know how you learn

People learn in different ways. Some understand best by reading and writing notes, others by listening and discussing, others by seeing diagrams, and many by doing the task with their hands. Most adults learn best by combining these: reading about calibrating a sprayer, watching the supervisor do it, and then doing it yourself while someone checks.

Useful study strategies

  • Preview: before a session, skim the learner guide to see what is coming.
  • Take notes: write key words, not full sentences. Use headings, bullets and abbreviations you understand.
  • Mind maps: put the main topic in the middle of a page and draw branches for sub-topics, such as ‘Soil’ with branches for texture, pH, organic matter and nutrients.
  • Link to work: after each lesson, think of one place on your farm where it applies.
  • Review: go over notes the same day and again a week later; regular short reviews beat one long session the night before an assessment.
  • Teach someone: explaining a topic to a colleague shows whether you really understand it.

Managing your time

Learners who work full time must plan. Use a simple weekly timetable: when you work, travel, rest, look after family, and when you study. Set small goals: ‘By Friday I will finish activity 4 in the learner guide.’ Tell your supervisor about assessment dates early so shifts can be arranged.

Language and learning

Many learner guides are in English, which may be your second or third language. Keep a personal word list of new terms with their meaning in your own words and in your home language. Technical words such as ‘germination’, ‘carcass’, ‘calibration’ or ‘traceability’ are part of your trade; learning them well makes you a more valuable worker.

lessons.title: Finding, using and sharing information
lessons.html:
Information sources

Learning programmes ask you to find information for assignments and projects. Sources include:

  • learner guides and textbooks;
  • workplace documents: SOPs, records, labels, manuals, policies;
  • people: supervisors, mentors, extension officers, vets, agronomists and experienced workers;
  • organisations: the Agricultural Research Council, industry bodies and government departments;
  • magazines, radio programmes and reliable websites.

Judging a source

Not all information is reliable. Ask: Who wrote it, and are they qualified? When was it written? Is it about South African conditions? Is it selling something? Information on social media or from a product advertisement must be checked against a reliable source. For legal or safety matters, use the official document or ask a qualified person.

Using information honestly

When you use information from a book, website or person in an assignment, put it in your own words and say where it came from, for example: ‘(Learner guide, Module 3, page 22)’ or ‘According to the farm's spraying SOP…’. Copying someone else's work and presenting it as your own is plagiarism. It is dishonest and can lead to your work being rejected.

Asking good questions

Asking questions is a skill. Be specific: instead of ‘I don't understand’, say ‘I don't understand how to work out the litres of water per hectare in step 3.’ Ask at the right time, write down the answer, and thank the person.

Group work

Many learning activities are done in groups. Good group members listen, share ideas, take on a role (leader, scribe, timekeeper, reporter), respect different opinions and do their part on time. When a group presents its findings, everyone should understand the answer, not only the reporter.

Communicating with facilitators and mentors

Your facilitator teaches, your workplace mentor guides you on the job, and an assessor judges your evidence. Keep them informed: tell them early if you are struggling, if you will miss a session, or if a workplace task for your logbook was not possible. Clear, polite, early communication solves most problems.

lessons.title: Assessment, portfolios and reflection
lessons.html:
Showing that you are competent

In outcomes-based learning you are assessed against standards. The result is competent or not yet competent. Not yet competent means you still need to show some outcomes, not that you have failed for ever. You can be reassessed after further learning.

Types of assessment

TypeExample
Knowledge testWritten or oral questions on the theory
Practical observationThe assessor watches you sample a seed lot or check carcass temperatures
Assignment or projectA report on water use in one orchard block
Workplace evidenceLogbook, records you completed, supervisor reports

Understanding assessment instructions

Read each question carefully and underline the instruction word:

  • List – give the items without explanation.
  • Describe – say what something is like or what happens.
  • Explain – give reasons: why or how.
  • Compare – show similarities and differences.
  • Calculate – show your working and the answer with units.

Check the marks or space given: a question worth 6 marks usually needs more than one sentence.

Building a portfolio of evidence

A portfolio of evidence (PoE) is a file that proves your competence. Keep it neat and organised: index, personal details, signed declarations, completed activities, workplace evidence and assessor feedback. Evidence must be valid (it shows the outcome), authentic (it is your own work), current and sufficient. Keep copies of everything.

Feedback and appeals

Read the assessor's feedback and ask about anything you do not understand. If you believe an assessment was unfair, you have the right to appeal through the provider's appeals procedure, calmly and in writing.

Recognition of prior learning

If you already have skills from years of work, recognition of prior learning (RPL) lets you be assessed on them without repeating all the training.

Reflection

After each module, write a few lines: What did I learn? What did I find difficult? How will I use it at work? Reflection turns experience into learning.

Key points

  • Combine reading, listening, seeing and doing, and review notes regularly.
  • Check sources for author, date, local relevance and bias, and acknowledge them.
  • Ask specific questions and communicate early with facilitators and mentors.
  • Understand instruction words such as list, explain and compare.
  • Keep a neat, authentic portfolio of evidence and reflect on your learning.
